body: I have never seen this message for non GUI apps like starship.
The certification process is for `.app` files. It doesn't apply to binary executables like starship.
I don't think this feature request is valid for a non-Mac app. Should this be closed?
Actually the ticket aint even featuring a real problem. Should be closed.

> I have never seen this message for non GUI apps like starship.

I did when I installed the Catalina beta, (forcing me to go from homebrew-ed starship to cargo-built starship), but as far as I can tell this is does not affect any production version of MacOS, else I expect we'd be swarmed by issues from our homebrew users.

If we discover that this is a problem on future versions of MacOS, we can reopen.

macOS certainly complains about being unable to check if the official starship build is secure on Big Sur (m1). Homebrew has their own build infrastructure anyway, but I remember reading something about them doing ad-hoc local-machine-only signing for downloaded binaries, which might be something that could be added to the official install script.

> Homebrew has their own build infrastructure anyway, but I remember reading something about them doing ad-hoc local-machine-only signing for downloaded binaries, which might be something that could be added to the official install script.

While this is true for Homebrew bluntly copying their solution won't result in a good experience because you lack important backstory there!

Buckle up because this is going to be a long journey...

First, a little refresher on how HB works. It either builds the stuff from source on a local machine or _pours bottles_ which is just a fancy name to unpack tarball with prebuilt binary/s, libs, packed manpages & headers, and so on. In typical user workflow bottles are favored over building from source and they get extracted to the so-called cellar (typically at `/usr/local/Cellar`) and symlinked back to `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/bin`, `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/lib`... respectively (where prefix is typically set to `/usr/local` and represents HB's installation location).
Now there is a catch! If the formula contains a library that is not needed by other formulas or things outside HB that library should be placed inside `libexec/lib` formula's bottle subdirectory (instead of `lib`) so it doesn't get symlinked back to the `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/lib` (`/usr/local/lib`) and clutter your FS hierarchy. Because dynamic library search path (`DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH`) is not really editable on macOS (due to SIP) Homebrew patches MachO binaries to fix dynamic library loading:
https://github.com/Homebrew/brew/blob/a930e2b3/Library/Homebrew/extend/os/mac/keg_relocate.rb#L61-L74 
Particular `libexec/lib` case is handled by https://github.com/Homebrew/brew/blob/a930e2b3/Library/Homebrew/extend/os/mac/keg_relocate.rb#L114-L115
Finally, it becomes clear why HB does it on the local machine, instead of doing it as part of their remote build process, once you take a look at the following table: https://docs.brew.sh/Formula-Cookbook#variables-for-directory-locations 
It shows that `libexec` is, in fact, indirectly calculated from `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX` environment variable value which is HB's installation location.

So long story short, **HB patches each and every MachO binary (and library) to make sure it is able to load dynamic libraries correctly and it has to be done after the bottle is poured (on a local machine) because new search paths are dependent on HB's install location ie `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX`.** 
I think it should be pretty clear now what is Misty talking about https://github.com/Homebrew/brew/issues/9082#issue-738557512 when she says:

> our tooling (such as ruby-macho) will break existing code signatures

because ruby-macho tooling does MachO patching in question.

As one thing leads to another, HB is forced to resign every binary on a local machine using an ad-hoc signature: https://github.com/Homebrew/brew/pull/9102#issue-518814468 with interesting possible improvements listed:

> Possible improvements:
> - only codesign if the macho file was previously signed? I don't know how we detect this
> - only codesign on ARM? I don't know if developer tools on Intel Big Sur codesign or not by default

meaning they certainly don't want to waste user time/resources (re)signing stuff if it isn't absolutely necessary! The keyword here is **resigning** which brings me to my final point.

What you proposed in #2413 is certainly a working solution/workaround but unfortunately, it doesn't make much sense. A better approach would be to obtain Apple distribution certificate and codesign binary once as a part of the release workflow instead of doing it on every download using end-user resources. Here is an example of one such workflow: https://localazy.com/blog/how-to-automatically-sign-macos-apps-using-github-actions

Furthermore, #2413 implies some unfortunate requirements for an installation script like having XCode Command Line Tools installed. In HB's case, this is fine because HB requires it anyway but in our case, it is simply one requirement too much :upside_down_face: 

**Finally, I'm proposing that we take one step back and rethink this thoroughly. My current take is that we should definitely avoid codesigning on the fly (on every download) and do it once as part of the release process.**

Also keep in mind that notarizing is primarily a security feature enabling Apple to provide users with a sense of security coming from a fact they can uniquely identify software and prevent malicious binaries from being (accidentally) run by checking its certificate. Using an ad-hoc signature weakens (or completely kills?) this contract and regardless of our personal preferences and thoughts about notarization, we shouldn't really take shortcuts there because some users might have strong feelings about security and they are ought to be respected.
I agree that a real code signing certificate is preferable, but I think ad-hoc signing provides an acceptable workaround in the meantime.
Why is an interim workaround needed? What prevents proper notarization workflow get established right away?

Has there been any further consideration for this feature request?

The company I work for has recently required that all OSX applications be signed & notarized, preventing us from using `starship` as it currently is. & while probably currently in the minority, I imagine this will be more common in the enterprise space as time goes on.

There has not been any further work on this at the moment. The only real blocker right now (afaik) is that none of the maintainers have had time to look into this.

I suppose [this action](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/xcode-notarize) might make a good starting point, but we need to ask questions like "whose account do we use?" and "how do we set up a system so that all maintainers can access it?"

Also note the project owners should be able to create an Apple Developer account for this project and have the annual fee waved since this project is free & open-source.

https://developer.apple.com/support/membership-fee-waiver/
If it helps at all.  The Fish Shell folks just threw their binary into a PKG and got it notarized. -> https://github.com/fish-shell/fish-shell

So I went ahead and bought myself an Apple Developer account, and it looks like this isn't quite as simple as I would have hoped.

Ignoring issues with Apple assuming that everything is built via XCode (requiring things like the hardened runtime), it looks like we can *notarize* a lot of stuff, but the notarization ticket can only be attached locally ("stapled", in Apple's parlance) to certain filetypes, those being DiskImages (dmg), PackageInstallers (.pkg) and app bundles (.app). Sadly, `.zip` files cannot be stapled.

When Gatekeeper encounters a program, it first looks to see if there's a notarization ticket stapled to the application. If not, it then tries to look the application up on the internet. If neither of those steps succeeds, then it will declare the application is un-notarized.

This means that if we just deliver binaries in a ZIP file, it is possible (though unlikely) that the user can download + install the program, but be unable to use it later because Gatekeeper cannot contact Apple's servers. I don't think an app bundle (.app) is appropriate for starship, which leaves us with .dmg or .pkg. Philosophically, I really don't like either of these for installing a single command-line binary tool, but it looks like if we want to have the property of "if you can install it, you can later use it," we'll need to provide one of those two methods.

> Also note the project owners should be able to create an Apple Developer account for this project and have the annual fee waved since this project is free & open-source.
> 
> https://developer.apple.com/support/membership-fee-waiver/

Thanks for the link! Unfortunately, it turns out that Apple's requirement for a fee waiver is "you must be an organization with a tax identification number and the ability to enter into legally-binding agreements." That's a pretty tall bar to clear--I'm not sure if *any* of the main Rust command-line projects meet that requirement. I'm not even sure if Rust itself could have met that requirement before the establishment of the Foundation.

Okay.

[starship.zip](https://github.com/starship/starship/files/8000712/starship.zip)

This is a ZIP archive containing (I think!) a notarized version of starship built off of `master`. At least, `spctl -a -vvv -t install starship` and `codesign --test-requirement="=notarized" --verify --verbose starship` both appear to tell me it's notarized. I've hit enough weird edge cases trying to get this done that I'd like someone else to verify it for me, in case some local caching thing is messing with me.

In the event that you want to make sure that nobody's messed with the archive, here's a gpg-signed version:

[starship.gpg.zip](https://github.com/starship/starship/files/8000722/starship.gpg.zip)

You should be able to download that, then run the following commands to get my public key from GitHub and verify the signature:

```
unzip starship.gpg.zip
curl https://github.com/chipbuster.gpg | gpg --import
gpg --verify starship.gpg
```

If someone else can verify that this binary appears to be notarized, our next step will be for me to figure out how to export some of these keys and get a GitHub Actions workflow set up.

Verified notarized.  I'm not sure I understand your reluctance to use a .pkg.  It makes perfect sense to me.  You want to distribute software, you wrap it in an installer.  For those of us in environments managed by a MDM (_Common at pretty much every university_), software provided in a package installer jives very well.  I realize it's just a CLI tool, but it still makes things easier.  Especially when it comes to uninstalling.  PKGs leave behind a receipt for admins to key off of for removing software.

> PKGs leave behind a receipt for admins to key off of for removing software.

This was actually one of my concerns. I'm not too familiar with `.pkg` capabilities--I've only dealt with them from stuff I've occasionally downloaded from websites, so it's safe to say have a very incomplete view of what they can actually do.

The other question I have is: can you easily change their install destination? My experience has been that you can't, but my guess is that there's an MDM tool that lets you modify the manifest files to change the install path? I would still prefer to also offer a .zip version for personal installs, but if `.pkg` works well for managed deployments I'd be happy to publish one as well.

`pkgutil --pkgs`

Will show you a list of all receipts on your box.  Lots of other fun arguments on that command to get info.

In general, yes you can change the install path of a package **IF** the installer was built to allow it.  Admins can then leverage a choice XML file to make the adjustment.  More commonly it's used for picking which components of a package to install.  For instance, the unified MS Office installer.  One could use a choice xml to only install Word and Powerpoint instead of everything.  Whether a MDM supports choice xmls varies.  I believe [Jamf](https://www.jamf.com) does not but [Munki](https://github.com/munki/munki) does.  Don't quote me on Jamf.

Agreed it's nice to offer multiple ways to obtain and install.  Having that notarized PKG option would be a huge awesome/thank you for me.

Fascinatingly, it seems that .pkg installers are completely undocumented by Apple. Even searching the Apple Developer Program documentation produces no results.

I did find this page which seems to be the closest thing to authoritative documentation on the file format, along with links to the (scant) other documentation available on the web and the appropriate manpages on OSX. Linking it here for easy referencing in the future: https://matthew-brett.github.io/docosx/flat_packages.html
This should be available with the first release newer than 1.3.0!

Not 100% sure what's going on, but I'll take a look and see if I can't get it fixed. In the meantime, I've manually uploaded the pkg files to the release page, so you can use those if you need a notarized binary right away.
